claim: Gene expression evolution through gene regulatory network (GRN) changes has gained appreciation as a driver of morphological evolution.
source: Gene expression evolution through gene regulatory network (GRN) changes has gained appreciation as a driver of morphological evolution.
evidence: This is a general statement about the field's current understanding, supported by established scientific consensus.

claim: The ancestral transcription factor activity of Bab gained a role in sculpting sex-specific pigmentation through the evolution of binding sites in a CRE of the pigment-promoting yellow gene.
source: Here, we show that the ancestral transcription factor activity of Bab gained a role in sculpting sex-specific pigmentation through the evolution of binding sites in a CRE of the pigment-promoting yellow gene.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by multiple experimental approaches including gel shift assays, reporter gene assays, and comparative analyses.

claim: A new trait can evolve by incorporating existing transcription factors into a GRN through CRE evolution.
source: This work demonstrates how a new trait can evolve by incorporating existing transcription factors into a GRN through CRE evolution, an evolutionary path likely to predominate newly evolved functions of transcription factors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings of the study, representing an inference about evolutionary mechanisms.

claim: Transcription factors play central roles in the development and evolution of animal traits by binding to cis-regulatory elements to spatially and temporally regulate patterns of gene expression.
source: Transcription factors play central roles in the development and evolution of animal traits by binding to cis-regulatory elements to spatially and temporally regulate patterns of gene expression (Davidson, 2006; Levine, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature in the field.

claim: The melanic pigmentation of the dorsal cuticle tergites covering the A5 and A6 abdominal segments of males has been inferred to be a novelty that evolved in the D. melanogaster lineage after it diverged from an ancestral monomorphically pigmented lineage within the Sophophora subgenus.
source: The melanic pigmentation of the dorsal cuticle tergites covering the A5 and A6 abdominal segments of males has been inferred to be a novelty that evolved in the D. melanogaster lineage after it diverged from an ancestral monomorphically pigmented lineage within the Sophophora subgenus (Jeong et al., 2006).
evidence: This evolutionary inference is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The Hox gene Abd-B plays an important role in activating the expression of terminal enzyme genes that are required for pigment formation.
source: Within the GRN controlling this trait, the Hox gene Abd-B plays an important role in activating the expression of terminal enzyme genes that are required for pigment formation (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1 which illustrates the GRN, and is part of established knowledge about this system.

claim: The yellow gene is activated through a CRE known as the 'body element' that possesses at least two binding sites for the Hox factor Abd-B.
source: One enzyme, encoded by the yellow gene is activated through a CRE known as the 'body element' (Camino et al., 2015; Wittkopp et al., 2002) that possesses at least two binding sites for the Hox factor Abd-B (Jeong et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work that characterized the body element and Abd-B binding sites.

claim: In D. melanogaster females, yellow expression is repressed in the A5 and A6 segments through its regulation by the tandem duplicate bab1 and bab2 genes.
source: In D. melanogaster females, yellow expression is repressed in the A5 and A6 segments through its regulation by the tandem duplicate bab1 and bab2 genes (Figure 2A) (Jeong et al., 2006), collectively referred to as Bab.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and reference to Figure 2A showing the gene duplication.

claim: Both bab1 and bab2 paralogs encode proteins that possess a conserved BTB domain that functions in homodimerization and heterodimerization.
source: Both paralogs encode proteins that possess a conserved BTB domain that functions in homodimerization and heterodimerization, and a conserved domain with pipsqueak (psq) and AT-hook domains that together confer a similar in vitro DNA-binding capability (Lours et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work characterizing the protein domains.

claim: The bab paralogs possess a conserved domain with pipsqueak (psq) and AT-hook domains that together confer a similar in vitro DNA-binding capability.
source: Both paralogs encode proteins that possess a conserved BTB domain that functions in homodimerization and heterodimerization, and a conserved domain with pipsqueak (psq) and AT-hook domains that together confer a similar in vitro DNA-binding capability (Lours et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Amino acid identity between bab1 and bab2 is 78% for the BTB domain and conserved domain, but drops to ~26% throughout the remainder of these proteins.
source: In contrast to the 78% amino acid identity observed for both BTB and conserved domain of the paralogs, amino acid identity drops to ~26% throughout the remainder of these proteins (Couderc et al., 2002) (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by citation and reference to source data showing the sequence comparison.

claim: A high amino acid identity exists between the conserved domains of the D. melanogaster paralogs and the Bab orthologs for the mosquito A. gambiae and honeybee A. mellifera.
source: Elsewhere, it was reported that a high amino acid identity exists between the conserved domains of the D. melanogaster paralogs and the Bab orthologs for the mosquito A. gambiae and honeybee A. mellifera, and most of the amino acid differences being conservative (Lours et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The Bab proteins are suspected to function as transcription factors.
source: Although the Bab proteins are suspected to function as transcription factors, no direct targets of regulation are known (Jeong et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated as a suspicion based on protein structure, with citation noting the lack of known direct targets.

claim: No direct targets of Bab regulation were known prior to this study.
source: Although the Bab proteins are suspected to function as transcription factors, no direct targets of regulation are known (Jeong et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated explicitly with citation to previous work.

claim: Bab expression evolved from a monomorphic pan-abdominal pattern to a sexually dimorphic expression pattern in which both paralogs are female-limited and absent from males during the latter half of pupal development.
source: In the lineage of D. melanogaster, Bab expression is suspected to have evolved from a monomorphic pan-abdominal pattern to a sexually dimorphic expression pattern in which both paralogs are female-limited, and absent from males during the latter half of pupal development when enzymes of the pigmentation GRN are deployed (Kopp et al., 2000; Salomone et al., 2013).
evidence: This evolutionary inference is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The dimorphic pattern of Bab expression required changes to two CREs controlling Bab's abdominal epidermis expression.
source: This dimorphic pattern of Bab expression required changes to two CREs controlling Bab's abdominal epidermis expression (Williams et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The yBE0.6 CRE drives male-limited GFP reporter transgene expression in the dorsal epidermis of the A5 and A6 abdominal segments.
source: We sought to characterize how Bab1 exerts its influence on a minimal 0.6 kb body element CRE (yBE0.6) (Camino et al., 2015) (Figure 2B) that drives male-limited GFP reporter transgene expression in the dorsal epidermis of the A5 and A6 abdominal segments (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is supported by citation and reference to Figure 2C and D showing the reporter expression pattern.

claim: The yBE0.6 reporter transgene activity matches the spatial, sex-limited, and temporal pattern of abdominal expression of yellow.
source: This reporter transgene activity matches the spatial, sex-limited, and temporal pattern of abdominal expression of yellow (Camino et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The SM4 and SM10 mutant CREs showed increased expression in the A5 and A6 segments of females.
source: While 8 of 10 'scanning mutant' CREs showed wild type reporter repression in the female abdomen (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), we observed increased expression in the A5 and A6 segments of the SM4 and SM10 mutants (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: The increased expression was more pronounced when the SM4 and SM10 mutations were combined in the same reporter.
source: Moreover, the increased expression was more pronounced when the SM4 and SM10 mutations were combined in the same reporter (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The SM4 and SM10 CRE sub-regions are required to suppress yellow expression in the posterior female abdomen.
source: These results identified two CRE sub-regions that are required to suppress yellow expression in the posterior female abdomen, likely through the recruitment of a transcriptional repressor protein.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing increased expression when these regions are mutated.

claim: When Bab1 was ectopically expressed in the dorsal midline of the male abdomen, yBE0.6 reporter expression was largely suppressed.
source: When Bab1 was ectopically expressed in the dorsal midline of the male abdomen by the GAL4/UAS system (Brand and Perrimon, 1993; Calleja et al., 2000), yBE0.6 reporter expression was largely suppressed (Figure 2H and I).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2H and I.

claim: A yBE0.6 CRE containing the SM4 and SM10 mutations was unresponsive to ectopic Bab1 expression.
source: However, a yBE0.6 CRE containing the SM4 and SM10 mutations, was unresponsive to ectopic Bab1 expression (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: The SM4 and SM10 CRE regions encode inputs that respond to regulation by Bab proteins.
source: These data reveal that the SM4 and SM10 CRE regions encode inputs that respond to regulation by Bab proteins.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing loss of Bab responsiveness when these regions are mutated.

claim: The DNA-binding domain (DBD) of Bab1 and Bab2 bound to similar DNA sequences.
source: Previously, it was shown that the DNA-binding domain (DBD) of Bab1 and Bab2 bound to similar DNA sequences (Lours et al., 2003); therefore, we chose to perform our experiments with the Bab1 DBD.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The Bab1 DBD substantially bound to the third probe of the SM4 region.
source: Of the three regions, only the third probe was substantially bound by the Bab1 DBD (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This is supported by gel shift assay data shown in Figure 3C-E.

claim: The binding of Bab1 DBD to the SM4 region third probe was DNA-sequence specific.
source: This binding was DNA-sequence specific, as a scanning mutant probe version failed to similarly shift (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by gel shift assay data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The 25 base pair segment of SM4 region three possesses a site or sites capable of Bab1 DNA-binding.
source: Thus, it seems likely that this 25 base pair segment possesses a site or sites capable of Bab1 DNA-binding.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the gel shift assay data.

claim: The Bab1 DBD preferably bound A/T-rich sequences, specifically those with TAA or TA repeats.
source: A previous study showed that the Bab1 DBD preferably bound A/T-rich sequences, specifically those with TAA or TA repeats (Lours et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: A TA > GA mutant probe that removed each TA motif was not noticeably bound by the Bab1 DBD.
source: We created a TA > GA mutant probe that removed each TA motif. This probe was not noticeably bound by the Bab1 DBD indicating that some or all these motifs are necessary features of a Bab1 binding site or sites (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by gel shift assay data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The sub2 probe of SM4 region three that spanned nine base-pairs and disrupted two of the TA motifs was not noticeably shifted by Bab1 DBD.
source: However, the sub2 probe that spanned nine base-pairs and disrupted two of the TA motifs was not noticeably shifted (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is supported by gel shift assay data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Gel shift assays support a direct Bab1 binding mechanism to suppress the yBE0.6 CRE sequence.
source: Collectively, this set of gel shift assays supports a direct Bab1 binding mechanism to suppress this CRE sequence (Figure 3A, red sequence).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the gel shift assay data.

claim: Mobility shifts were observed for the first and third regions of SM10 when tested with Bab1 DBD.
source: We tested three overlapping sub element regions for an interaction with the Bab1 DBD (Figure 4C–E), and observed mobility shifts for the first and third regions (Figure 4C and E).
evidence: This is supported by gel shift assay data shown in Figure 4C and E.

claim: A scanning mutant version of the SM10 third region was bound, albeit to a lesser extent, by Bab1.
source: A scanning mutant version of the third region was bound, albeit to a lesser extent, by Bab1 (Figure 4G), indicating that this in vitro binding was not sequence-specific or that the mutant probe created a weak Bab-binding site.
evidence: This is supported by gel shift assay data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: A scan mutant probe of SM10 first region was not noticeably bound by the Bab1 DBD.
source: Therefore, we focused our attention on the first region for which a scan mutant probe was not noticeably bound by the Bab1 DBD (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by gel shift assay data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The sub3 mutant probe of SM10 first region showed little-to-no binding by Bab1 DBD.
source: While each mutant probe appeared to be bound to a lesser extent than the wild type probe, the sub3 mutant probe showed little-to-no binding (Figure 4J).
evidence: This is supported by gel shift assay data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: The results suggest the presence of at least one additional Bab-binding site in the SM10 region.
source: These results suggest the presence of at least one additional Bab-binding site in the SM10 region.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the gel shift assay data.

claim: Bab1 functions as a DNA-binding transcription factor that interacts with at least two sites within the yBE0.6 CRE and thereby represses the expression of this CRE in the female abdomen where Bab1 is highly expressed.
source: Collectively, our results support a direct model of regulation in which Bab1 functions as a DNA-binding transcription factor that interacts with at least two sites within the yBE0.6 CRE and thereby represses the expression of this CRE in the female abdomen where Bab1 is highly expressed.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of experimental evidence including gel shift assays and reporter gene assays.

claim: The bab genes have been shown to be sufficient to suppress D. melanogaster tergite pigmentation when ectopically expressed.
source: While the bab genes have been shown to be sufficient to suppress D. melanogaster tergite pigmentation when ectopically expressed (Couderc et al., 2002; Kopp et al., 2000), the individual necessities of bab1 and bab2 paralogous genes have not been fully resolved.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The individual necessities of bab1 and bab2 paralogous genes have not been fully resolved prior to this study.
source: While the bab genes have been shown to be sufficient to suppress D. melanogaster tergite pigmentation when ectopically expressed (Couderc et al., 2002; Kopp et al., 2000), the individual necessities of bab1 and bab2 paralogous genes have not been fully resolved.
evidence: This is stated explicitly as a gap in knowledge.

claim: The bab1 shmiR transgene containing the siRNA id #3 sequence led to a conspicuous increase in the dorsal medial pigmentation of the female A5 and A6 tergites.
source: Relative to the control (Figure 5A), the bab1 shmiR transgene containing the siRNA id #3 sequence (Table 1) led to a conspicuous increase in the dorsal medial pigmentation of the female A5 and A6 tergites (Figure 5B), whereas the transgene including the siRNA id #4 sequence (Table 1) resulted in a phenotype not noticeably different from that of the negative control (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The individual ectopic expression of the shmiR transgenes containing either the siRNA id #12 or #16 sequences for bab2 resulted in ectopic dorsal medial tergite pigmentation in females.
source: For bab2, the individual ectopic expression of the shmiR transgenes containing either the siRNA id #12 or #16 sequences (Table 2) resulted in ectopic dorsal medial tergite pigmentation in females (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: Suppression of tergite pigmentation in D. melanogaster females requires individual contributions from both bab1 and bab2.
source: Hence, these results demonstrate that suppression of tergite pigmentation in D. melanogaster females requires individual contributions from both bab1 and bab2.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RNAi experiments showing that knockdown of either paralog increases pigmentation.

claim: Chained shmiR transgenes co-expressing bab1 and bab2 shmiRs resulted in more expansive ectopic pigmentation phenotypes when ectopically expressed in the dorsal midline.
source: We found that these chained shmiR transgenes, when ectopically expressed in the dorsal midline resulted in more expansive ectopic pigmentation phenotypes (Figure 5F and G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5F and G.

claim: For one chained combination, ectopic pigmentation included the A4 tergites of males and females.
source: Notably, for one chained combination, ectopic pigmentation included the A4 tergites of males and females (Figure 5F, red arrowheads).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The pupal male abdomen lacks significant bab1 and bab2 expression.
source: Not surprisingly, the RNAi phenotypes were most extreme in the female abdomen as the pupal male abdomen lacks significant bab1 and bab2 expression (Salomone et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Both bab1 and bab2 are sufficient to suppress male tergite pigmentation when ectopically expressed.
source: Previous studies have shown that both bab1 and bab2 are sufficient to suppress male tergite pigmentation when ectopically expressed (Couderc et al., 2002; Kopp et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Leaky expression of UAS-bab1 and UAS-bab2 transgenes resulted in reduced pigmentation of the male A5 and A6 tergites.
source: In the absence of a GAL4 driver, leaky expression of these transgenes resulted in reduced pigmentation of the male A5 and A6 tergites (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: Ectopic expression of the bab1 ORF driven by pnr-GAL4 was lethal in adult males.
source: When we drove ectopic expression of these ORFs in the dorsal midline by the pnr-GAL4 chromosome, we failed to recover viable adult males which possessed the UAS-bab1 ORF transgene, indicating that the ectopic-expression phenotype was lethal.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental crosses.

claim: Ectopic expression of bab2 ORF driven by pnr-GAL4 eliminated tergite pigmentation in the dorsal midline of males and caused a non-specific split tergite phenotype in both males and females.
source: While we obtained fewer than expected offspring with ectopic expression of the bab2 ORF than expected for independent assortment (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), some adults were identified. For these specimens, tergite pigmentation was eliminated in the dorsal midline of males, and a non-specific split tergite phenotype was seen for both males and females (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: bab1 and bab2 have a strong pigment-suppressing capability.
source: These outcomes show that bab1 and bab2 have a strong pigment-suppressing capability, although in the genetic background tested, bab1 ectopic expression was lethal.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ectopic expression experiments.

claim: Leaky expression of the bab1 DBM was insufficient to suppress tergite pigmentation.
source: We found that leaky expression of the bab1 DBM was insufficient to suppress tergite pigmentation (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Ectopic expression of the Bab1 DBM by the pnr-GAL4 driver resulted in detectable accumulation of nuclear protein which did not induce lethality or a pigmentation phenotype.
source: Moreover, ectopic expression of the Bab1 DBM by the pnr-GAL4 driver resulted in detectable accumulation of nuclear protein (Figure 6—figure supplement 4) which did not induce lethality or a pigmentation phenotype (Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplements 1, 2, and 4.

claim: Expression of the Bab1 DBM in the y-GAL4 pattern resulted in males with the wild type melanic tergites.
source: Similarly, expression of the Bab1 DBM in the y-GAL4 pattern resulted in males with the wild type melanic tergites (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: DNA binding is required for the D. melanogaster Bab paralogs to repress tergite pigmentation.
source: Collectively, these results lend further support to a model in which DNA binding is required for the D. melanogaster Bab paralogs to repress tergite pigmentation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments with the DNA-binding mutant.

claim: Dimorphic pigmentation is thought to have derived from a monomorphic ancestral state in the lineage of D. melanogaster after it diverged from that for D. willistoni and perhaps even as recently as the D. pseudoobscura split in the Sophophora subgenus.
source: The stark dimorphism between the melanic pigmentation of D. melanogaster male and female abdominal tergites represents a trait whose origin has now been resolved to the level of its GRN connections. Dimorphic pigmentation is thought to have derived from a monomorphic ancestral state in the lineage of D. melanogaster after it diverged from that for D. willistoni and perhaps even as recently as the D. pseudoobscura split in the Sophophora subgenus (Jeong et al., 2006; Salomone et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an evolutionary inference supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Leaky expression from the attP2 genomic site of D. willistoni bab1 and D. mojavensis bab2 transgenes resulted in a similar reduction in male A5 and A6 tergite pigmentation as D. melanogaster orthologs.
source: As seen for the D. melanogaster ORF transgenes, leaky expression from the attP2 genomic site of transgene insertion resulted in a similar reduction in male A5 and A6 tergite pigmentation (Figure 6D D. willistoni bab1; and 6E, D. mojavensis bab2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6D and 6E.

claim: Pigmentation was dramatically suppressed when D. willistoni bab1 and D. mojavensis bab2 orthologous proteins were ectopically expressed in the dorsal medial midline pattern of pnr-GAL4 and y-GAL4.
source: Pigmentation was dramatically suppressed when these orthologous proteins were ectopically expressed in the dorsal medial midline pattern of pnr-GAL4, (Figure 6—figure supplement 2) and y-GAL4 (Figure 6J D. willistoni bab1; and 6K, D. mojavensis bab2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2, Figure 6J, and Figure 6K.

claim: The ability of the Bab1 and Bab2 proteins to regulate dimorphic pigmentation did not require the evolution of an altogether new biochemical capability.
source: These results suggest that the ability of the Bab1 and Bab2 proteins to regulate dimorphic pigmentation did not require the evolution of an altogether new biochemical capability.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the functional equivalence of orthologs from different species.

claim: The origin of the Bab1 and Bab2 paralogs likely resulted from a duplication event that occurred in the evolutionary history of the Dipteran order.
source: The origin of the Bab1 and Bab2 paralogs likely resulted from a duplication event that occurred in the evolutionary history of the Dipteran order (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic distribution of the paralogs, supported by reference to Figure 2A.

claim: All species of fruit flies with sequenced genomes and the Tsetse fly Glossina morsitans possess bab1 and bab2 paralogs.
source: This scenario is supported by the findings that all species of fruit flies with sequenced genomes and the Tsetse fly Glossina morsitans possess bab1 and bab2 paralogs, whereas basally branching Dipteran species such as Anopheles (A.) gambiae and Aedes aegypti only possess a single paralog.
evidence: This is based on analysis of genomic data from multiple species.

claim: Basally branching Dipteran species such as Anopheles gambiae and Aedes aegypti only possess a single bab paralog.
source: This scenario is supported by the findings that all species of fruit flies with sequenced genomes and the Tsetse fly Glossina morsitans possess bab1 and bab2 paralogs, whereas basally branching Dipteran species such as Anopheles (A.) gambiae and Aedes aegypti only possess a single paralog.
evidence: This is based on analysis of genomic data from multiple species.

claim: The genomes of the flour beetle Tribolium castaneum and the moth Bombyx mori each possess a single bab gene.
source: Moreover, the genomes of the flour beetle Tribolium castaneum and the moth Bombyx mori, from orders closely related to Diptera, each possess a single bab gene.
evidence: This is based on analysis of genomic data from these species.

claim: Leaky expression of the A. gambiae bab gene resulted in reduced pigmentation in the male A5 and A6 tergites.
source: We found that like all other bab orthologs tested in this study, leaky expression of the A. gambiae bab gene resulted in reduced pigmentation in the male A5 and A6 tergites (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Forced ectopic expression of A. gambiae bab driven by pnr-GAL4 and y-GAL4 both resulted in more extensive repression of tergite pigmentation.
source: Moreover, forced ectopic expression driven by pnr-GAL4 and y-GAL4 both resulted in more extensive repression of tergite pigmentation (Figure 6—figure supplement 2, and Figure 6L).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2 and Figure 6L.

claim: The general functional capability of Bab proteins was ancient and has been conserved during the 100 million years or more since the gene duplication event occurred.
source: These outcomes are consistent with the interpretation that the general functional capability of these proteins was ancient and has been conserved during the 100 million years or more since the gene duplication event occurred.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the functional equivalence of orthologs from different species spanning a long evolutionary time.

claim: The further reduced pigmentation caused by the Bab1 orthologs compared to those for Bab2 and A. gambiae Bab suggests that incremental enhancements have occurred.
source: In fact, the further reduced pigmentation caused by the Bab1 orthologs compared to those for Bab2, and A. gambiae Bab suggests that such incremental enhancements have indeed occurred (Figure 6).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the quantitative effects of different orthologs shown in Figure 6.

claim: Drosophila and Anopheles orthologs were similarly capable of repressing reporter transgenes regulated by the yellow regulatory regions of both dimorphic species D. melanogaster and D. malerkotliana.
source: We observed the Drosophila and Anopheles orthologs were similarly capable of repressing reporter transgenes regulated by the yellow regulatory regions of both dimorphic species.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the reporter gene assays shown in Figure 7.

claim: The functional equivalency of distantly related Bab orthologs extends to the ability to regulate a derived target gene in a Drosophila lineage.
source: Thus, it can be concluded that the functional equivalency of distantly related Bab orthologs extends to the ability to regulate a derived target gene in a Drosophila lineage.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the reporter gene assays.

claim: Both D. melanogaster bab paralogs and orthologs from other fly and mosquito lineages can similarly impact the development of melanic tergite pigmentation when ectopically expressed in D. melanogaster.
source: Here, we showed that both D. melanogaster bab paralogs and orthologs from other fly and mosquito lineages can similarly impact the development of melanic tergite pigmentation when ectopically expressed in D. melanogaster (Figure 6), and each gene can induce a similar non-specific split tergite phenotype (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: For body pigment regulation, the protein coding regions of bab paralogs are functionally equivalent.
source: These outcomes suggest for at least for body pigment regulation, that their protein coding regions are functionally equivalent.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ectopic expression experiments.

claim: Some divergent patterns of expression have been found for the bab paralogs in D. melanogaster, consistent with a role for neo- or sub-functionalization.
source: In contrast to the conserved protein functionality that we observed for the Bab paralogs, some divergent patterns of expression have been found for the paralogs in D. melanogaster, consistent with a role for neo- or sub-functionalization (Couderc et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The majority of bab paralog expression patterns appear to be common to both paralogs.
source: Yet, the majority of bab paralog expression patterns appear to be common to both paralogs (Couderc et al., 2002; Rogers et al., 2013; Salomone et al., 2013), including the pupal abdominal epidermis, for which expression is governed by two shared CREs (Williams et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Heterozygous bab null females express a male-like pattern of tergite pigmentation compared to wild type females.
source: It has been found that heterozygous bab null females express a male-like pattern of tergite pigmentation compared to wild type females, and the homozygous null pigmentation phenotype is more or less equivalent to that of males. (Rogers et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The RNAi reduction of expression for either bab1 or bab2 resulted in more male-like pigmentation pattern on the female abdomen.
source: Here, we showed that the RNAi reduction of expression for either bab1 or bab2 resulted in more male-like pigmentation pattern on the female abdomen, and RNAi for both paralogs simultaneously resulted in a more pronounced male-like phenotype (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The need for a higher overall quantity of expressed Bab protein seems to be key for Bab's role in the GRN generating the derived dimorphic pattern of abdomen pigmentation.
source: While qualitative differences through CRE functional divergence must have occurred to drive the divergent paralog expression in some tissues, the need for a higher overall quantity of expressed Bab protein seems to be key for Bab's role in the GRN generating the derived dimorphic pattern of abdomen pigmentation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the RNAi experiments showing additive effects of knocking down both paralogs.

claim: One study provided data consistent with the scenario that Bab regulated the expression of pigmentation genes prior to the emergence of dimorphic trait, showing that Bab2 expression often, but not always, displayed an anti-correlation to where melanic pigmentation developed on fruit fly tergites, including non-Sophophora species.
source: One study provided data consistent with this scenario, showing that Bab2 expression often, but not always, displayed an anti-correlation to where melanic pigmentation developed on fruit fly tergites, including non-Sophophora species (Gompel and Carroll, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: An abdominal epidermis CRE activity is present in the yellow gene intron of the monomorphic pigmented species such as D. pseudoobscura, D. willistoni, and the non-Sophophoran species D. virilis.
source: Furthermore, it was demonstrated that an abdominal epidermis CRE activity is present in the yellow gene intron of the monomorphic pigmented species such as D. pseudoobscura, D. willistoni, and the non-Sophophoran species D. virilis (Kalay and Wittkopp, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The melanic species D. virilis expresses Bab1 and Bab2 throughout the male and female abdomens suggesting an inability of Bab to suppress pigmentation genes such as yellow in this species.
source: First, the melanic species D. virilis expresses Bab1 and Bab2 throughout the male and female abdomens suggesting an inability of Bab to suppress pigmentation genes such as yellow in this species (Salomone et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The regulation of yellow by Bab in D. melanogaster is limited to the body element CRE in which Bab binding sites were found.
source: Furthermore, the regulation of yellow by Bab in D. melanogaster is limited to the body element CRE in which we found Bab binding sites.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings of this study.

claim: Clearly identifiable orthologs to the D. melanogaster body element remain difficult to identify in more distantly related fruit fly species hailing from monomorphically pigmented lineages.
source: This is significant as clearly identifiable orthologs to the D. melanogaster body element remains difficult to identify in more distantly related fruit fly species hailing from monomorphically pigmented lineages (Figure 9A), although the wing element and its activity has remained well-conserved by comparison.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 9A.

claim: There is no evidence for an ancient linkage between Bab and an antecedent of the yellow body element.
source: Thus, there is no evidence for an ancient linkage between Bab and an antecedent of the yellow body element.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lack of sequence conservation in the body element across species.

claim: The activation of yellow in the male-specific spot that adorns the wings of D. biarmipes is bab-independent.
source: While an ancestral bab-yellow linkage may exist for a yet unidentified trait, the activation of yellow in the well-studied male-specific spot that adorns the wings of D. biarmipes is bab-independent (Arnoult et al., 2013; Gompel et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The D. melanogaster body element possesses derived binding sites for both Bab and the Hox factor Abd-B.
source: Finally, the D. melanogaster body element possesses derived binding sites for both Bab and the Hox factor Abd-B (Figure 9A) (Jeong et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by data from this study and citation to previous work, with reference to Figure 9A.

claim: It seems much more likely that Bab was integrated into an antecedent GRN to play a key role in differentiating the expression outcomes between males and females.
source: Based upon the available data, it seems much more likely that Bab was integrated into an antecedent GRN to play a key role in differentiating the expression outcomes between males and females.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the collective evidence presented in the study.

claim: The integration of Bab into the pigmentation GRN involved the remodeling of existing CREs controlling Bab expression in the abdominal epidermis and the acquisition of yellow as a direct target of regulation through the formation of binding sites in the emergent body element.
source: This integration involved the remodeling of existing CREs controlling Bab expression in the abdominal epidermis (Rogers et al., 2013; Williams et al., 2008), and the acquisition of yellow as a direct target of regulation through the formation of binding sites in the emergent body element (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the collective evidence, supported by citations and reference to Figure 9.

claim: D. pseudoobscura yellow body element CRE is mildly Bab-responsive.
source: One hint to this puzzle may lie in D. pseudoobscura, a species whose yellow body element CRE is mildly Bab-responsive (Figure 8 and Figure 8—figure supplement 1), but for which Bab expression retains its ancestral monomorphic expression.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8 and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: The capability to respond to Bab may have evolved first, followed by the evolution of dimorphic Bab expression patterns.
source: This might suggest that the capability to respond (albeit weakly) to Bab evolved first, followed by the evolution of dimorphic Bab expression patterns.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the D. pseudoobscura data.

claim: The gene tan, which is co-expressed with yellow, appears to have a very different encoding for dimorphism than yellow.
source: Further, the evolutionary connections identified here represent a subset of the connections downstream of Bab. While the yellow body CRE contains separable activating and repressing inputs, the gene tan, which is co-expressed with yellow appears to have a very different encoding for dimorphism (Camino et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Extensive mutagenesis of the tan MSE failed to find any mutations that relaxed dimorphic expression, suggesting that activating and repressing inputs are overlapping, or are closely situated in this CRE's DNA sequence.
source: Extensive mutagenesis of the tan MSE failed to find any mutations that relaxed dimorphic expression, suggesting that activating and repressing inputs are overlapping, or are closely situated in this CREs DNA sequence.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the mutagenesis results.

claim: The increased complexity of the dimorphic pigmentation GRN through the integration of the Bab transcription factors by CRE evolution will exemplify a common mechanism whereby increasingly sophisticated GRNs have come about to regulate traits throughout the animal kingdom.
source: We suggest that the increased complexity of the dimorphic pigmentation GRN through the integration of the Bab transcription factors by CRE evolution will exemplify a common mechanism whereby increasingly sophisticated GRNs have come about to regulate traits throughout the animal kingdom.
evidence: This is a speculative generalization based on the findings of this study.

claim: The vast majority of transcription factor binding specificities remain conserved over long evolutionary periods.
source: The vast majority of transcription factor binding specificities remain conserved over long evolutionary periods (Nitta et al., 2015), and many of these factors are functionally equivalent between distantly related taxa.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Many transcription factors are functionally equivalent between distantly related taxa.
source: The vast majority of transcription factor binding specificities remain conserved over long evolutionary periods (Nitta et al., 2015), and many of these factors are functionally equivalent between distantly related taxa.
evidence: This is a general statement about transcription factor evolution, supported by established knowledge.

claim: The origin of the male-specific pigmentation of D. melanogaster is an example where evolutionarily conserved transcription factors gained a new function through their integration into a GRN by CRE evolution.
source: Thus, the origin of the male-specific pigmentation of D. melanogaster is an example where evolutionarily conserved transcription factors gained a new function through their integration into a GRN by CRE evolution.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the collective findings of the study.

claim: The findings represent the first-documented direct target sites of the Bab proteins.
source: These findings represent the first-documented direct target sites of the Bab proteins, sites which arose coincident with the evolution of sexually dimorphic Bab expression patterns in the abdomen (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is stated explicitly as a novel finding of the study.

claim: The Bab binding sites arose coincident with the evolution of sexually dimorphic Bab expression patterns in the abdomen.
source: These findings represent the first-documented direct target sites of the Bab proteins, sites which arose coincident with the evolution of sexually dimorphic Bab expression patterns in the abdomen (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the evolutionary analysis, with reference to Figure 9B.

claim: Multiple tiers of a complex GRN evolved to produce a Hox-regulated trait while preserving the genetic toolkit of regulatory and differentiation genes.
source: Thus, our results provide a clear example in which multiple tiers of a complex GRN evolved to produce a Hox-regulated trait while preserving the genetic toolkit of regulatory and differentiation genes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the collective findings of the study.

claim: The D. melanogaster bab locus provides an interesting example in which the protein-coding and regulatory divergence of duplicated genes can be compared.
source: The D. melanogaster bab locus provides an interesting example in which the protein-coding and regulatory divergence of duplicated genes can be compared.
evidence: This is a general statement about the significance of the study system.

claim: Both bab paralogs have been maintained in the genomes of distantly related fruit fly species since the duplication event.
source: Since this duplication event, both bab paralogs have been maintained in the genomes of distantly related fruit fly species (Clark et al., 2007; Richards et al., 2005), and in species from related families whose genomes have been sequenced (Giraldo-Calderón et al., 2015; Kriventseva et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to genomic studies.

claim: Both D. melanogaster bab paralogs and orthologs from other fly and mosquito lineages can induce a similar non-specific split tergite phenotype.
source: Here, we showed that both D. melanogaster bab paralogs and orthologs from other fly and mosquito lineages can similarly impact the development of melanic tergite pigmentation when ectopically expressed in D. melanogaster (Figure 6), and each gene can induce a similar non-specific split tergite phenotype (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: For body pigment regulation, the protein coding regions of bab paralogs appear to be functionally equivalent.
source: These outcomes suggest for at least for body pigment regulation, that their protein coding regions are functionally equivalent.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ectopic expression experiments.

claim: Heterozygous bab null females express a male-like pattern of tergite pigmentation compared to wild type females, and the homozygous null pigmentation phenotype is more or less equivalent to that of males.
source: It has been found that heterozygous bab null females express a male-like pattern of tergite pigmentation compared to wild type females, and the homozygous null pigmentation phenotype is more or less equivalent to that of males. (Rogers et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: RNAi for both bab paralogs simultaneously resulted in a more pronounced male-like phenotype than RNAi for either paralog alone.
source: Here, we showed that the RNAi reduction of expression for either bab1 or bab2 resulted in more male-like pigmentation pattern on the female abdomen, and RNAi for both paralogs simultaneously resulted in a more pronounced male-like phenotype (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The D. melanogaster wing element showed a slight reduction in activity when in the presence of ectopic Bab1 or Bab2 compared to the Bab1 DBM control.
source: While the D. melanogaster wing element showed a slight reduction in activity when in the presence of ectopic Bab1 or Bab2 compared to the Bab1 DBM control, no apparent reduction in activity was observed for the transgenes with either the D. malerkotliana, D. pseudoobscura, or D. willistoni yellow regulatory sequences (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: No apparent reduction in wing element activity was observed for the transgenes with either the D. malerkotliana, D. pseudoobscura, or D. willistoni yellow regulatory sequences in the presence of ectopic Bab.
source: While the D. melanogaster wing element showed a slight reduction in activity when in the presence of ectopic Bab1 or Bab2 compared to the Bab1 DBM control, no apparent reduction in activity was observed for the transgenes with either the D. malerkotliana, D. pseudoobscura, or D. willistoni yellow regulatory sequences (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: The regulatory activity of the D. malerkotliana yellow regulatory region showed greater level of repression (33 ± 0% and 33 ± 1% in the presence of ectopic Bab1 or Bab2, respectively) than for D. melanogaster (56 ± 1% and 53 ± 0% in the presence of ectopic Bab1 and Bab2, respectively).
source: One being the even greater level of regulatory-activity repression for the D. malerkotliana yellow regulatory region (33 ± 0% and 33 ± 1% in the presence of ectopic Bab1 or Bab2, respectively) than for D. melanogaster (56 ± 1% and 53 ± 0% in the presence of ectopic Bab1 and Bab2, respectively).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the reporter gene assays.

claim: The regulatory activity of the D. pseudoobscura CRE was modestly repressed in the presence of Bab (85 ± 2% and 70 ± 1% in the presence of ectopic Bab1 and Bab2, respectively).
source: Second, the regulatory activity of the D. pseudoobscura CRE was modestly repressed in the presence of Bab (85 ± 2% and 70 ± 1% in the presence of ectopic Bab1 and Bab2, respectively).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the reporter gene assays.

claim: Expression of the bab1 and bab2 ORFs driven by the y-GAL4 transgene eliminated both lethality and tergite developmental defects, resulting in male adults which entirely lacked melanic pigmentation on the A5 and A6 tergites.
source: Expression of the bab1 and bab2 ORFs driven by the y-GAL4 chromosome eliminated both lethality and tergite developmental defects, resulting in male adults which entirely lacked melanic pigmentation on the A5 and A6 tergites (Figure 6G and H).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6G and H.

claim: Bab1 and Bab2 are both potent suppressors of pigmentation in two very different regimes of ectopic expression.
source: These data show that Bab1 and Bab2 are both potent suppressors of pigmentation in two very different regimes of ectopic expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ectopic expression experiments using different GAL4 drivers.

claim: The Bab1 and Bab2 proteins possess a conserved domain that includes both pipsqueak (psq) and AT-Hook motifs that function as an in vitro DNA-binding domain or DBD.
source: The Bab1 and Bab2 proteins possess a conserved domain that includes both pipsqueak (psq) and AT-Hook motifs that function as an in vitro DNA-binding domain or DBD (Lours et al., 2003), supporting the notion that these paralogs function as transcription factors in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Bona fide direct targets of either Bab1 or Bab2 have yet to be discovered prior to this study.
source: However, bona fide direct targets of either Bab1 or Bab2 have yet to be discovered.
evidence: This is stated explicitly as a gap in knowledge prior to this study.

claim: The Bab1 DBD failed to bind DNA in vitro when possessing non-synonymous mutations in the pipsqueak (psq) motif converting Alanine and Isoleucine amino acids to Glycine and Proline, respectively (AI576GP).
source: Previously, it was shown that the Bab1 DBD failed to bind DNA in vitro when possessing non-synonymous mutations in the pipsqueak (psq) motif converting Alanine and Isoleucine amino acids to Glycine and Proline, respectively (AI576GP), or when non-synonymous mutations altered a stretch of Arginine, Glycine, and Arginine amino acids in the AT-Hook motif to Aspartic acid, Glycine, and Aspartic acid (RGR627DGD), respectively (Lours et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The Bab1 DBD failed to bind DNA in vitro when non-synonymous mutations altered a stretch of Arginine, Glycine, and Arginine amino acids in the AT-Hook motif to Aspartic acid, Glycine, and Aspartic acid (RGR627DGD).
source: Previously, it was shown that the Bab1 DBD failed to bind DNA in vitro when possessing non-synonymous mutations in the pipsqueak (psq) motif converting Alanine and Isoleucine amino acids to Glycine and Proline, respectively (AI576GP), or when non-synonymous mutations altered a stretch of Arginine, Glycine, and Arginine amino acids in the AT-Hook motif to Aspartic acid, Glycine, and Aspartic acid (RGR627DGD), respectively (Lours et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The regulatory activities of the yellow 5' sequences were imaged at ~85 hAPF, a time point when endogenous yellow expression occurs in the abdominal epidermis.
source: The regulatory activities of the yellow 5' sequences were imaged at ~85 hAPF, a time point when endogenous yellow expression occurs in the abdominal epidermis (Camino et al., 2015; Jeong et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a methodological detail supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Melanic tergite pigmentation requires the specific expression of the pigmentation genes yellow and tan, while blocking the expression of the yellow-pigment promoting ebony gene.
source: Melanic tergite pigmentation requires the specific expression of the pigmentation genes yellow and tan, while blocking the expression of the yellow-pigment promoting ebony gene.
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 1 and represents established knowledge about the pigmentation pathway.

claim: Abd-B is not expressed in the anterior A2-A4 segments and resultantly yellow and tan lack the direct and indirect activating input.
source: Abd-B is not expressed in the anterior A2-A4 segments and resultantly yellow and tan lack the direct and indirect activating input.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and represents established knowledge about the GRN.

claim: In the anterior A2-A4 segments, Abd-A acts as a direct repressor of tan in combination with (direct or indirect) repressive effects of exd and hth.
source: In these anterior segments, Abd-A acts as a direct repressor of tan in combination with (direct or indirect) repressive effects of exd and hth.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and represents established knowledge about the GRN.

claim: Abd-B is expressed in the posterior A5 and A6 segments, where it functions as a direct activator of yellow and an indirect activator of tan.
source: Abd-B is expressed in the posterior A5 and A6 segments, where it functions as a direct activator of yellow and an indirect activator of tan.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and represents established knowledge about the GRN.

claim: In the posterior A5 and A6 segments, Abd-A acts as an indirect activator of tan.
source: In these segments, Abd-A acts as an indirect activator of tan.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and represents established knowledge about the GRN.

claim: In the female abdomen, Bab acts as a dominant repressor of yellow and tan expression, overriding the presence of Abd-B and Abd-A.
source: In the female abdomen, Bab acts as a dominant repressor of yellow and tan expression, overriding the presence of Abd-B and Abd-A.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and represents established knowledge about the GRN.

claim: An ancestral bab gene was duplicated into the paralogous bab1 and bab2 genes in a Dipteran lineage that includes Drosophila fruit flies.
source: An ancestral bab gene was duplicated into the paralogous bab1 and bab2 genes in a Dipteran lineage that includes Drosophila fruit flies.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A and is an inference based on phylogenetic distribution.

claim: Male-specific expression of yellow in the abdominal epidermis is under the control of the yBE0.6 CRE that possesses two binding sites for Abd-B.
source: Male-specific expression of yellow in the abdominal epidermis is under the control of the yBE0.6 CRE that possesses two binding sites for Abd-B that are shown as yellow rectangles.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B and is supported by previous work.

claim: Blue bars delimit the SM4 and SM10 regions required to suppress CRE activity in females.
source: Blue bars delimit the SM4 and SM10 regions required to suppress CRE activity in females.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B and is a finding of this study.

claim: The yBE0.6 EGFP reporter transgene is elevated in the male A5 and A6 abdomen segments but is only barely detected in females.
source: The yBE0.6 EGFP reporter transgene is elevated in the male A5 and A6 abdomen segments (C) but is only barely detected females (D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: Ectopic reporter expression occurs in the female abdomen when either the SM4, SM10, or both regions are mutated.
source: Ectopic reporter expression occurs in the female abdomen when either the SM4, SM10, or both regions are mutated.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E-G.

claim: The pnr-GAL4 driver activates dorsal midline expression of the UAS-EGFP gene, demarcating its domain of misexpression.
source: The pnr-GAL4 driver activates dorsal midline expression of the UAS-EGFP gene, demarcating its domain of misexpression.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Dorsal midline expression of the yBE0.6 CRE is lost when bab1 is ectopically expressed by pnr-GAL4.
source: Dorsal midline expression of the yBE0.6 CRE is lost when bab1 is ectopically expressed by pnr-GAL4.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2I.

claim: When the SM4 and SM10 regions are mutated, the yBE0.6 CRE can activate reporter expression in midline regions in spite of ectopically expressed bab1.
source: When the SM4 and SM10 regions are mutated, the yBE0.6 CRE can activate reporter expression in midline regions in spite of ectopically expressed bab1.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2J.
